chief_complaint: wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness following closed midshaft humerus fracture
hpi_details: 32M sustained midshaft humerus fracture in motor vehicle collision presenting with acute inability to extend wrist/MCP joints and radial sensory loss.
ideas: He thinks the broken bone in his upper arm pinched or crushed the main nerve leading to his hand during the car crash.
concerns: He is worried that the nerve damage is permanent and that his hand will remain paralyzed, leaving him unable to work with his hands or manage daily chores.
expectations: He hopes to be fitted with a supportive wrist splint to keep his hand functional and find out whether the nerve will recover naturally without another surgery.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Radial nerve palsy secondary to humeral shaft fracture evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Radial nerve palsy secondary to humeral shaft fracture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes expectant management with serial neurovascular exams for the typical neurapraxic palsy, reserving surgical exploration for specific red-flag scenarios, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness following closed midshaft humerus fracture
Key HPI features: 32M sustained midshaft humerus fracture in motor vehicle collision presenting with acute inability to extend wrist/MCP joints and radial sensory loss.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals stable. Closed midshaft humerus deformity with tenderness, swelling, and crepitus, no open wound. Wrist, MCP, and thumb extension absent (wrist drop); sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Wrist flexion, finger flexion, and intrinsic hand strength preserved. Radial and ulnar pulses palpable, capillary refill normal, compartments soft.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Radial nerve palsy secondary to humeral shaft fracture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Brachial plexus injury without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Wrist drop (motor deficit).
management_principles: Perform and document a detailed neurovascular exam (wrist/finger/thumb extension, radial sensory distribution, distal pulses) before and after any fracture manipulation
Most closed-fracture radial nerve palsies are neurapraxic and recover spontaneously; manage expectantly with serial exams and a wrist-extension splint for functional support
Reserve early surgical exploration for palsy occurring after fracture reduction/manipulation, an open fracture, or failure to recover by 3-4 months (consider EMG/nerve conduction studies)
Immobilize the fracture and refer to orthopedics for definitive management (functional bracing versus operative fixation).
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Radial Nerve Palsy Humeral Shaft Fracture: wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness following closed midshaft humerus fracture. 32M sustained midshaft humerus fracture in motor vehicle collision presenting with acute inability to extend wrist/MCP joints and radial sensory loss.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals stable. Closed midshaft humerus deformity with tenderness, swelling, and crepitus, no open wound. Wrist, MCP, and thumb extension absent (wrist drop); sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Wrist flexion, finger flexion, and intrinsic hand strength preserved. Radial and ulnar pulses palpable, capillary refill normal, compartments soft.
reference_soap.assessment: Closed midshaft humeral shaft fracture with associated radial nerve palsy, most consistent with neurapraxia given the closed low-energy mechanism.
reference_soap.plan: Immobilize the arm in a coaptation splint or functional humeral brace and obtain dedicated humerus radiographs (including elbow and shoulder) to fully characterize the fracture. Because most closed-fracture radial nerve palsies are neurapraxic and recover spontaneously within 3-4 months, manage expectantly with serial neurovascular exams and a wrist-extension splint for functional support. Refer to orthopedics for fracture management and reserve early surgical exploration for palsy after fracture manipulation, an open fracture, or failure to recover by 3-4 months (consider EMG/nerve conduction studies at that point).

teaching.diagnosis: Radial nerve palsy secondary to humeral shaft fracture
teaching.one_liner: 32M with a midshaft humerus fracture from an MVC, now with wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness.
red_flags: Sensory loss in radial nerve distribution

must_ask.say: Can you describe how the accident happened and how your arm was injured?
Can you lift your wrist and fingers up like this?
Where exactly do you feel numbness on your hand?

must_ask.objective: Ask about timing of nerve symptoms relative to injury
must_ask.say: Did the wrist weakness start right at the time of injury, or after the cast/splint was applied?

must_ask.objective: Explain the expectant management and monitoring plan
must_ask.say: Many radial nerve injuries with this fracture recover over weeks to months, but the orthopedic team will monitor your strength, sensation, and circulation closely.

history.answer: I was in a car crash earlier today and broke my right upper arm, and now my right wrist is completely limp and I can't lift my hand.
It is both. I can't lift my wrist or fingers at all, and the skin on the back of my hand feels completely numb.
It is only in my right hand and wrist, especially the back of my hand near my thumb. My left arm and both legs feel completely normal.
It happened suddenly right at the moment of the crash a few hours ago. My arm and hand were completely normal before that.
It has stayed completely limp since the crash. It hasn't gotten any better or worse.
I can't lift my hand to grab anything or button my shirt because my wrist just flops down, though I can still squeeze my fingers closed.
Any movement of my broken upper arm causes sharp pain, but the wrist drop and numbness stay the same regardless of position or rest.
No, my neck and back feel fine, and I don't have any pain shooting down my spine or legs.
No slurred speech, no facial drooping, no blurred or double vision, and no dizziness at all.
No, my bladder and bowel control are completely normal, and I have normal sensation around my private area.
No shortness of breath, no trouble chewing or swallowing, and no drooping eyelids.
No, I haven't noticed any muscle twitching, and my muscles haven't shrunken because this just happened today.
No, I haven't had a cold, fever, cough, or diarrhea recently.
No high blood pressure, no diabetes, no high cholesterol, and no heart problems like an irregular heartbeat.
I don't have diabetes, I have never had stomach or bowel surgery, and I eat a regular diet with meat and vegetables.
I am not taking any prescription medications, water pills, steroids, or chemotherapy.
No, I work at an office desk and don't do heavy vibrating tool work or lean heavily on my elbows.
I was the driver in a car accident earlier today; another vehicle struck my side and my right arm slammed hard against the car door frame.
I can bend my wrist and fingers downward into a fist, but I cannot extend my wrist upward or straighten my fingers and thumb at all.
The numbness is on the back of my right hand, right in the web space between my thumb and index finger; my palm feels normal.
My wrist went limp immediately after the bone broke in the crash, before anyone tried to splint or move it.
When my arm snapped in the crash, I think the jagged bone must have pinched or severed the nerve that controls my wrist and fingers.
I'm terrified that this nerve damage is permanent and my hand is going to stay limp like this forever, which would mean I can never go back to work.
I hope you can give me a brace to hold my wrist up so my hand isn't just hanging there, and tell me if this nerve will wake back up on its own.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had surgery and have never been hospitalized before this accident.
I don't take any regular medications, vitamins, or supplements.
I have no allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially on occasion, maybe a beer or two a month, and had nothing to drink today.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 78 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert young male in moderate distress holding his right arm across his abdomen; no facial asymmetry or respiratory distress.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact with symmetric facial expression, clear speech, normal visual fields, and intact extraocular movements.
Visible swelling, deformity, localized tenderness, and bony crepitus over the right midshaft humerus; skin is intact with no open wounds or punctures.

Right wrist drop with complete inability to extend wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints, and thumb (0/5); intact right wrist flexion, finger flexion, and hand intrinsic strength (5/5); full strength in left arm and both legs.
Marked decrease to light touch and pinprick sensation over the dorsal aspect of the right first web space; normal sensation over the palmar hand, median/ulnar distributions, and contralateral arm.
Right brachioradialis reflex is diminished; right triceps and biceps reflexes are preserved; symmetric normal knee and ankle reflexes with downgoing toes bilaterally.
Right radial and ulnar pulses are strong and palpable at 2+; brisk capillary refill under two seconds and right forearm compartments are soft.
No midline cervical or lumbar tenderness; negative Spurling test and negative straight-leg raise test bilaterally.
